transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, I came in because... well, I just can’t make myself go near the front windows at work anymore. Or even that part of the street, really. I keep finding excuses to just stay in the back room, even though being out on the floor is a big part of my job. I just can't go near there.
When you think about going near those front windows or that part of the street, what exactly are you afraid will happen?

I'm not really sure, honestly. Um... it's not like I have a specific thing in my head that I think is going to happen. I just... I don't know. I look at that area and I just get this really strong feeling that I can't go over there. I don't really know what I'm expecting to happen, I just know I can't do it.
When did you first start feeling this way about the front windows and that area? Can you remember what happened around that time?

It's been about two weeks now. Um, it started right after... well, I was working an overnight shift at the store, and a car crashed right through the front window. So, yeah, it's been going on ever since that happened.
Besides the windows and that street area, are there other situations or places that make you feel similarly anxious or that you've been avoiding?

Um... not really, no. It's just the front of the store, mostly. I mean, I guess I get a little jumpy if I hear a really loud noise or tires screeching, but I don't think I've been avoiding anything else. It's just that spot at work where it happened.
Since the car crashed through the window two weeks ago, have you been having unwanted memories or flashbacks of that event coming back to you, even when you don't want them to?

Yeah, I have. The crash just keeps popping into my head out of nowhere. Like, I'll be trying to set up displays or just doing my job, and suddenly it's right there again. I can actually hear that huge bang and see the glass coming down... it feels like it's happening all over again right in front of me.
Have you been having trouble sleeping since the accident, or experiencing nightmares about the crash?

No, my sleep has been okay, actually. I mean, it takes me a little bit to wind down after a shift, but once I'm asleep, I stay asleep. And I haven't had any nightmares about the crash or anything like that.

Besides getting jumpy at loud noises, have you noticed that you're more on edge or alert than usual in general? Like, do you find yourself scanning your surroundings more, or feeling like you need to be ready for something bad to happen?

Um, no, I don't think so. I haven't really noticed feeling on edge all the time, and I'm not, like, constantly scanning the room or anything. It's really just the loud noises that startle me, or being right at that spot by the window at work. But other than that, no, I don't feel like I'm walking around waiting for something bad to happen.

Besides the crash itself and avoiding that area at work, have you noticed any other changes in how you feel or think about things in general over these past two weeks? For example, do you find yourself feeling more worried or anxious about things in everyday life, or has your mood changed in other ways?

Not really, no. I mean... I feel pretty normal otherwise. I'm not really worrying about everyday stuff any more than I usually do, and my mood hasn't really changed. It's just... yeah, just what I mentioned about the loud noises and being at work. Everything else is basically the same.
Since the crash happened two weeks ago, have you noticed that you feel kind of numb or detached from things around you, or like you're not really present or aware of what's going on?

Yeah, actually, I have noticed that a little bit. Sometimes when I'm out on the sales floor, things just feel... kind of weird. Like the overhead lights and all the clothing racks feel really far away and just fake, somehow. 

It's hard to explain, but it almost feels like I'm watching myself move through the store instead of really being there in my own body. So, yeah, I guess I do get that detached feeling sometimes.
When you have those flashbacks of the crash, do you find yourself trying hard not to think about it or pushing the memory away, or do you try to avoid talking about what happened?

No, I don't really do that. When the memory pops up, it just kind of happens... I don't actively try to push it away or block it out. And I don't mind talking about it, either. I mean, I've told my family and some of my coworkers about the crash. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm trying to avoid thinking or talking about it.

You mentioned feeling detached and like you're watching yourself move through the store. Have you noticed that you're having trouble remembering important details about the actual moment the car crashed through the window, or does the memory of what happened feel fuzzy or unclear to you?

No, I remember everything pretty clearly. It's not fuzzy at all. I can remember exactly where I was standing, the sound of the glass shattering, and exactly what the car looked like when it came through. So, no, I'm not having any trouble remembering the details of it.
Since the crash happened, have you noticed that you feel less emotional about things in general, or that it's harder to feel happy or sad about things the way you normally would?

No, I wouldn't say that. I still feel things normally, I think. Like, I still laugh at jokes with my coworkers and I get annoyed when things go wrong at work... I don't feel numb emotionally, just that weird detached feeling I mentioned earlier. But as far as being happy or sad, that hasn't really changed.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with acute stress disorder following a direct traumatic exposure (car crash through storefront window 2 weeks ago). She exhibits the core features: intrusive flashbacks with sensory details (hearing the bang, seeing glass), avoidance of the specific trauma-related location (front windows/street), hyperarousal to trauma-related stimuli (startle response to loud noises/tire screeching), and depersonalization/derealization symptoms (feeling detached, watching herself move through the store). Symptom onset was immediate post-trauma, duration is 2 weeks (within the 3-day to 1-month window for ASD), and there is clear functional impairment (avoiding significant work duties). Notably absent are: sleep disturbance, nightmares, avoidance of trauma discussion, emotional numbing, or generalized hypervigilance—features that would be more typical of PTSD. The symptom profile and acute timeline are consistent with Acute Stress Disorder (F43.10).
